plan.angle: Keep the structure, but fix the second payoff. Use the JAMA primary results (treatment-regimen estimand). Trial 1, no PAP: average AHI change about −18 events an hour on orforglipron vs about −4.5 on placebo. Trial 2, using PAP: about −17 vs about −5. Card: 'Adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more · 52 weeks · orforglipron (highest dose each person tolerated) vs placebo'. Use percentage reductions, remission-or-mild figures and weight change only if the full paper prints them, with the paper's definition and estimand. Otherwise drop them. Chapter 5: 'Lilly said on 9 November 2026 that it plans to ask the FDA to approve it for sleep apnea. Asking for approval isn't approval.' Call trial figures 'adverse events', for example 'gastrointestinal adverse events: 68% vs 37% on placebo in the trial without PAP'. Keep the CPAP don't-stop line, the prescriber line and the watch-next target (ssb7Zcs3KSY).
plan.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron) for Sleep Apnea: What Did the Trial Show?
plan.why: Exp I fast-turn: a peer-reviewed phase 3 RCT for a drug people search by name, with low creator competition (the EloraTZP pattern), and it feeds the Foundayo What to Expect video. | fact-check: The topic checks out. The JAMA paper exists: Malhotra et al., ATTAIN-OSA, 'Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials', published online 9 Nov 2026 (jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2856406). It reports two 52-week phase 3 double-blind trials in adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more. Trial 1 had 363 people not using PAP. Trial 2 had 349 people using PAP. Lilly's press release of 9 Nov 2026 says it plans to submit to the FDA by the end of 2026, so the drug is not approved for OSA. One instruction in the angle is wrong. It says to avoid 'the 17–18 figure from the press', but −17.8 and −17.3 events/h are the JAMA paper's own primary results (treatment-regimen estimand). Trial 1: orforglipron −17.8 vs placebo −4.5 (difference −13.2). Trial 2: −17.3 vs −5.3 (difference −12.0). The 43.8%, −21.1 events/h and 31.5% remission-or-mild figures come from Lilly or a different estimand. Use them only if they are in the paper, and name the estimand. The abstract does not give weight change or say how AHI was measured in the PAP trial. Get both from the full text, or leave them out. GI adverse events in the abstract: 68.0% vs 37.4% (Trial 1) and 70.6% vs 36.6% (Trial 2). Call them 'gastrointestinal adverse events'. Name the arm 'orforglipron at the highest dose each person tolerated'. Don't list mg values or anything that reads like a dosing ladder. Population: 'obesity or overweight' (BMI 27 or more), not 'obesity' only. Zepbound's OSA approval covers adults with obesity. Keep it to one neutral line with no comparison. The Foundayo Medication Guide (Revised: 7/2026) pancreatitis wording is confirmed: 'severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting'.

package.description:
Foundayo (orforglipron) and sleep apnea: two randomized trials tested it against placebo. Sleep apnea is not an approved use of Foundayo.

Safety note: Don't stop CPAP or any other sleep apnea treatment on your own. Talk to your prescriber or sleep specialist first.

Quick answer: In adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and a BMI of 27 or more, orforglipron (highest tolerated dose) lowered the apnea-hypopnea index by an average of about 18 events an hour vs about 4.5 with placebo in the trial without PAP, and about 17 vs about 5 in the trial of PAP users, over 52 weeks (JAMA, ATTAIN-OSA). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common than on placebo.

Sources:
1. Malhotra A, et al. Orforglipron for OSA: Results From 2 RCTs (ATTAIN-OSA). JAMA, published online 9 Nov 2026. jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2856406
2. Foundayo Prescribing Information, Section 1 (Revised 7/2026). uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html

IG instagram.com/informedlab · TikTok tiktok.com/@informedlab · FB facebook.com/InforMedLab

#Orforglipron

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
package.pinned_comment: In the trial without CPAP, orforglipron lowered breathing events (AHI) by an average of about 18 an hour vs about 4.5 with placebo over 52 weeks, in adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and a BMI of 27 or more. Sleep apnea is not an approved use of Foundayo, and a pill isn't a CPAP swap: don't stop CPAP on your own. Save this for your next appointment. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

scenes.narration: A sleep test counts those moments. The count is called the AHI, short for apnea-hypopnea index.

scenes.narration: An apnea is a pause in breathing that lasts at least ten seconds.

scenes.narration: A hypopnea is a stretch of shallow breathing that comes with a dip in oxygen or a brief arousal from sleep.

scenes.narration: Add both kinds together, divide by the hours you slept, and you get events per hour.

scenes.narration: Five to fifteen an hour counts as mild. Fifteen to thirty is moderate. More than thirty is severe.

scenes.narration: Thirty an hour works out to one breathing event every two minutes, all night long.

visual.stock_query: clock ticking over sleeper

scenes.narration: So everyone in these trials started at moderate or worse. In the trial without CPAP, the average drop on orforglipron, before comparing with placebo, was about eighteen fewer stalls or shallow stretches each hour.

scenes.narration: Over seven hours of sleep, eighteen fewer an hour would add up to more than a hundred fewer events. That is our own multiplication of the raw drop, not a trial result and not the gap versus placebo, but it shows why the number matters.

scenes.narration: Obstructive sleep apnea happens when the airway at the back of your throat narrows or closes while you sleep.

scenes.narration: Think of the airway like a soft drinking straw. Press on it from the outside, and less air gets through.

visual.stock_query: soft straw being squeezed, air bubbles

scenes.narration: Your throat muscles relax during sleep. Extra weight can add fat around the neck and tongue, and that can crowd the airway further.

scenes.narration: But weight is only one piece. Age, family history, the shape of your face and jaw, or large tonsils can matter too, so people of any size can have sleep apnea.

scenes.narration: And untreated, it is linked to high blood pressure, heart problems, and the kind of daytime sleepiness that can make driving risky.

scenes.narration: The good news is that it is an airway problem, not a character flaw, and it is treatable.

scenes.narration: So where does weight come in? Researchers in Wisconsin tested the sleep of several hundred adults, then tested them again about four years later.

script.cta: After the CPAP payoff and the three-question checklist, there's one subscribe ask tied to a clear benefit: "If you want GLP-one trials explained this clearly, without the hype, subscribe. We break down each big result in plain words." The video ends with "There is a video I would watch next, linked in the description." Post-note watch-next target: Foundayo (Orforglipron) What to Expect (ssb7Zcs3KSY). The publisher adds the verified link, and line 1 of the description stays empty for it. If the description or captions quote the Medication Guide's pancreatitis sentence, use its exact wording and keep the drug name outside the quotation marks. S2 link: keep https://investor.lilly.com/node/55271. If the publisher's link check fails, use the mirror https://lilly.gcs-web.com/node/55271.

factcheck.summary: Everything checked matches the sources, and the video is safe. ATTAIN-OSA (JAMA, Malhotra et al., 9 Nov 2026) confirms every trial figure in the script. Both trials were 52-week, phase 3, double-blind and placebo-controlled, and enrolled adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more. Mean AHI change was −17.8 vs −4.5 without PAP (gap −13.2) and −17.3 vs −5.3 with PAP (gap −12.0). GI adverse events were 68.0% vs 37.4% and 70.6% vs 36.6%. Participants took the highest dose each person tolerated, and the main analyses use the treatment-regimen estimand. The Foundayo label (Rev 7/2026) confirms that OSA is not an approved use and that the drug acts on the GLP-1 receptor. Lilly's release, confirmed through search coverage, says it plans to file for moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight by the end of 2026. The Zepbound label (Revised 11/2026) confirms its OSA approval. The Peppard 2000 study confirms 690 Wisconsin adults, about 4 years of follow-up, and +32% / −26% for 10% weight change, and the script correctly calls it observational. The NHLBI pages support the explanation of how sleep apnea works, its risk factors and its risks. The script's own multiplication is labelled as ours, and the hypothetical Rosa is clearly introduced with "imagine". There is no dosing advice, the CPAP don't-stop line is present, and the prescriber line is present. Only small wording fixes remain.

issues.claim: "stop taking it and get medical help right away, and let your healthcare provider know"
issues.problem: The Foundayo Medication Guide's own pancreatitis sentence, as read from Lilly's US label page, says: "Stop taking FOUNDAYO and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting." The script uses the channel's fixed emergency line but cites it to S4 as if it were the guide's wording. The safety meaning is fine, but the attribution is looser than the guide's text.
issues.fix: Keep the channel's fixed line, but make the list card match the guide's sentence: item 3 becomes "Stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away." If the description or captions quote the guide, use the guide's exact wording and keep the drug name outside the quotation marks.

issues.claim: "the shape of your jaw or tonsils can matter too"

issues: headline 'A PILL FOR APNEA?' wraps to 3 lines but still readable at phone size
'2 TRIALS' is less emotionally engaging, reads as dry/informational rather than curiosity-driven

thumbnail.reasoning: None of the three give away the answer, show mismatched emotion, or repeat the title verbatim, so no hard caps apply. All keep proper hedging ('NOT APPROVED'/'NOT AN APPROVED USE YET') and are legible at phone size. #1 ('2 TRIALS') is accurate and credible but the number-focused hook is the least emotionally charged of the three — it reads more like a stat card than a hook that taps into the fear of sleep apnea. #0 ('A PILL FOR APNEA?') has a cute, high-contrast mascot and a clear curiosity gap tied to the drug being a pill, which is engaging, but the cheerful cartoon pill character slightly undercuts the seriousness of a sleep-apnea audience's concern. #2 ('FEWER PAUSES?') has the strongest single focal point — a bold black lung silhouette with a large yellow question mark against a high-contrast purple background — and directly names the felt problem (breathing pauses at night) without resolving it, which best matches the emotional pull of a health-curious/worried viewer while staying fully accurate and non-misleading. It also carries the drug name and approval-status subtext clearly. Legibility is excellent across all phone/small sizes. I'm picking #2 as the best combination of CTR potential and clean legibility.

issues.fix: Replace with: "orforglipron (highest tolerated dose) lowered the apnea-hypopnea index by an average of about 18 events an hour vs about 4.5 with placebo"

issues.claim: orforglipron lowered breathing events (AHI) by about 18 an hour vs about 4.5 with placebo over 52 weeks
issues.problem: Same missing measure (average) as in the description. The script frames it as an average, not a promise.

That's a close phonetic match for a new brand name, every other scene was heard correctly, word error is low (final 0.013), masking is clean at 0.013 and the captions come from the script, so it isn't a broken narration.
